presentation: PRESENTATION: , Patient, 13 years old, comes to your office with his mother complaining about severe ear pain.  He awoke during the night with severe ear pain, and mom states that this is the third time this year he has had earaches.,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  ,Patient reports that he felt good after taking antibiotics with each earache episode and has recently started on the wrestling team.  Mom reports that patient has been afebrile with each of the earache episodes, and he has not had upper respiratory symptoms.  Patient denies any head trauma associated with wrestling practice.,BIRTH AND DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY:,  Patient's mother reports a normal pregnancy with no complications, having received prenatal care from 12 weeks.  Vaginal delivery was uneventful with a normal perinatal course.  Patient sat alone at 6 months, crawled at 9 months, and walked at 13 months.  His verbal and motor developmental milestones were as expected.,FAMILY/SOCIAL HISTORY: , Patient lives with both parents and two siblings (brother - age 11 years, sister - age 15 years).  He reports enjoying school, remains active in scouts, and is very excited about being on the wresting team.  Mom reports that he has several friends, but she is concerned about the time required for the wrestling team.  Patient is in 8th grade this year and an A/B student.  Both siblings are healthy.  His Dad has hypertension and has frequent heartburn symptoms that he treats with over-the-counter (OTC) medications.  Mom is healthy and has asthma.,PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  ,Patient has been seen in the clinic yearly for well child exams.  He has had no major illnesses or hospitalizations.  He had one emergency room visit 2 years ago for a knee laceration.  Patient has been healthy except for the past year when he had two episodes of otitis media not associated with respiratory infections.  He received antibiotic therapy (amoxicillin) for the otitis media and both episodes resolved without problems.  Patient's Mom states that he takes no prescribed medications or OTC medications, but he admits that he has been taking his dad's OTC Pepcid AE sometimes when he gets heartburn.  Upon further examination, he reports taking Pepcid when he eats pizza or Mexican food.  He does complain of sore throats sometimes and often feels burning in his throat when he goes to sleep at night after a late evening snack.,NUTRITIONAL HISTORY: , Patient eats cereal bars or pop tarts with milk for breakfast most days.  He takes his lunch (usually a sandwich and chips or yogurt and fruit) for lunch.  Mom or his sister cooks supper in the evening.  The family goes out to eat once or twice a week and he only gets "fast food" once or twice a week according to his Mom.  He says he eats "a lot" especially after a wrestling meet.,PHYSICAL EXAM:,Height/weight:  Patient weighs 109 pounds (60th percentile) and is 69 inches tall (93rd percentile).  He is following the growth pattern he established in infancy.,Vital signs:  BP 110/60, T 99.2, HR 70, R 16.,General:  Alert, cooperative but a bit shy.,Neuro:  DTRs symmetric, 2+, negative Romberg, able to perform simple calculations without difficulty, short-term memory intact.  He responds appropriately to verbal and visual cues, and movements are smooth and coordinated.,HEENT:  Normocephalic, PEERLA, red reflex present, optic disk and ocular vessels normal.  TMs deep red, dull, landmarks obscured, full bilaterally.  Post auricular and submandibular nodes on left are palpable and slightly tender.,Lungs:  CTA, breath sounds equal bilaterally, excursion and chest configuration normal.,Cardiac:  S1, S2 split, no murmurs, pulses equal bilaterally.,Abdomen:  Soft, rounded, reports no epigastric tenderness but states that heartburn begins in epigastric area and rises to throat.  Bowel sounds active in all quadrants.  No hepatosplenomegaly or tenderness.  No CVA tenderness.,Musculoskeletal:  Full range of motion, all extremities.  Spine straight, able to perform jumping jacks and duck walk without difficulty.,Genital:  Normal male, Tanner stage 4.  Rectal exam - small amount of soft stool, no fissures or masses.,LABS:  ,Stool negative for blood and H. pylori antigen.  Normal CBC and urinalysis.  A barium swallow and upper GI was scheduled for the following week.  It showed marked GE reflux.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT: , The differential diagnoses for patient included (a) chronic otitis media/treatment failure, (b) peptic ulcer disease/gastritis, (c) gastro esophageal reflux disease (GERD) or carbonated beverage syndrome, (d) trauma.,CHRONIC OTITIS MEDIA. , Chronic otitis media due to a penicillin resistant organism would be the obvious diagnosis in this case.  It is rare for an adolescent to have otitis media with no precipitating factor (such as being on a swim team or otherwise exposed to unusual organisms or in an unusual environment).  It is certainly unusual for him to have three episodes in 1 year.,PEPTIC ULCER DISEASE.,  There were no symptoms of peptic ulcer disease, a negative H. pylori screen and lack of pain made this diagnosis less likely.  Trauma.  Trauma was a possibility, particularly since adolescent males frequently minimize symptoms especially if they might limit participation in a sport but patient maintained that he had not had an event where he struck his head or neck and that he always wore his helmet with ear padding.,GERD.,  The history of "heartburn" relieved by his father's medication was striking.  The positive study supported the diagnosis of GERD, which was severe and chronic enough to cause irritation of the mucosal surfaces exposed to the gastric juices and edema, inflammation in the inner ears.,PLAN:,  Patient and his Mom agreed to a trial of omeprazole 20 mg at bedtime for 2 weeks.  Patient was to keep a diary of any episodes of heartburn, including what foods seemed to aggravate it.  The clinician asked him to avoid using any antacid products in the meantime to gage the effectiveness of the medication.  He was also given a prescription for 10 days of Augmentin99 and a follow-up appointment for 2 weeks.  At his follow-up appointment he reported one episode after he ate a whole large pizza after wrestling practice but said it went away pretty quickly after he took his medication.  A 6-month follow up appointment was scheduled.

human_dx_summary: The primary diagnosis is chronic otitis media caused by a penicillin resistant organism, with GERD as a significant contributing factor, while peptic ulcer disease and trauma are less likely.

**ASSESSMENT**

1. **Acute Otitis Media (AOM), bilateral:** The patient presents with acute, severe ear pain. Otoscopic examination reveals bilateral deep red, dull, and full tympanic membranes with obscured landmarks, accompanied by tender left post-auricular and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Given that this is his third episode this year, this is classified as recurrent AOM. 
2. **Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD):** The patient has classic symptoms of heartburn, nocturnal throat burning, and sore throats, which are exacerbated by late-night snacks and specific trigger foods (e.g., pizza, Mexican food). This clinical picture is corroborated by the recent upper GI/barium swallow demonstrating marked GE reflux. Notably, untreated GERD can cause microaspiration or inflammation that contributes to Eustachian tube dysfunction, which may be a predisposing factor for his recurrent otitis media in the absence of upper respiratory infections.

**PLAN**

**1. Acute Otitis Media:**
*   **Medications:** Prescribe Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) 875 mg/125 mg PO BID for 10 days. (Chosen over standard amoxicillin due to the recurrent nature of the infection, ensuring adequate coverage for potential beta-lactamase-producing organisms).
*   **Symptomatic Relief:** Ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO every 6–8 hours as needed for ear pain. 
*   **Follow-up:** Return to the clinic in 48–72 hours if symptoms do not improve, or sooner if they worsen (e.g., development of fever, worsening pain, or post-auricular erythema/swelling suggestive of mastoiditis).

**2. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD):**
*   **Lifestyle Modifications:** Avoid eating or drinking (except water) within 2–3 hours of bedtime. Elevate the head of the bed by 6–8 inches. Identify and limit known trigger foods (e.g., spicy foods, tomato-based sauces, high-fat foods). 
*   **Medications:** Initiate Omeprazole 20 mg PO daily, taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast, for an 8-week therapeutic trial. Explicitly counsel the patient and mother to discontinue the use of the father's OTC Pepcid (famotidine) and to only use medications prescribed specifically for the patient.
*   **Referrals:** Consider referral to Pediatric Gastroenterology if symptoms persist after an 8-week trial of PPI therapy and lifestyle modifications, or immediately if alarm symptoms develop (e.g., dysphagia, odynophagia, unintended weight loss, or GI bleeding).

**3. General Counseling and Preventive Care:**
*   **Medication Safety:** Reinforce the importance of not sharing prescription or over-the-counter medications among family members.
*   **Nutrition/Hydration:** Encourage continued healthy eating habits and adequate hydration, particularly given the increased physical demands and weight-class considerations of the wrestling team.
*   **Follow-up:** Schedule a routine follow-up visit in 4 weeks to assess the resolution of the ear infection, evaluate the response to GERD therapy, and determine if an Otolaryngology (ENT) referral is warranted for consideration of tympanostomy tubes should the ear infections continue to recur despite optimized medical management.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, well-controlled:** Hemoglobin A1c is 6.4% on minimal pharmacologic therapy (Metformin 500 mg daily). 
2. **Obesity (Class I):** BMI is 31.5. 
3. **Dietary counseling for weight reduction:** Patient is attempting highly restrictive diets (currently a restrictive vegetarian diet lacking fruits, grains, starchy vegetables, and adequate protein) for weight loss. She has expressed concerns regarding the risk of hypoglycemia and whether weight loss will cure her diabetes.

*Clinical Reasoning:* The patient's current HbA1c indicates excellent glycemic control. Her risk of severe hypoglycemia on her current restrictive diet is very low, as she is only taking metformin, an insulin sensitizer that does not typically cause hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy. However, her current "veggie diet" is nutritionally unbalanced, lacks essential macronutrients and micronutrients, and is unlikely to be sustainable long-term. Her morning hyperglycemia is likely related to evening caloric and carbohydrate intake (the "dawn phenomenon" exacerbated by late/large evening meals). While significant weight loss can improve insulin sensitivity and potentially lead to diabetes remission, this is best achieved through a sustainable, balanced caloric deficit rather than extreme dietary restriction.

**PLAN:**

1. **Medications:** 
   - Continue Metformin 500 mg daily. Reassured the patient that this medication carries a minimal risk of hypoglycemia, even with dietary changes. No dosage adjustments are needed at this time.

2. **Diet and Nutrition:** 
   - Advised against continuing the highly restrictive "veggie diet" due to the high risk of nutritional deficiencies and lack of long-term sustainability. 
   - Reinforced the recommended 1,200-calorie balanced meal plan discussed during the visit, emphasizing the inclusion of lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, controlled portions of whole grains, and healthy fats.
   - Educated the patient on the importance of evening portion control and avoiding large, late-night meals to help mitigate her morning fasting hyperglycemia.

3. **Patient Education:** 
   - Discussed realistic expectations regarding diabetes remission. Explained that while significant, sustained weight loss can dramatically improve glycemic control and sometimes lead to remission, it requires a balanced, lifelong lifestyle modification rather than short-term, extreme dietary restriction.

4. **Monitoring:** 
   - Continue home blood glucose monitoring. Specifically advised checking fasting morning levels and 2-hour post-prandial levels after dinner to help guide appropriate evening meal adjustments.

5. **Follow-up & Testing:** 
   - Return to clinic in 3 months for a weight check, review of dietary adherence and home glucose logs, and a repeat Hemoglobin A1c to ensure continued glycemic control. 
   - No additional imaging or laboratory studies are indicated at this time, aligning with high-value, cost-conscious care.
llm_dx_summary: The patient has well-controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus on minimal pharmacologic therapy, complicated by Class I obesity and an unsustainable, nutritionally unbalanced restrictive vegetarian diet.

**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Symptomatic midline incisional hernia:** Approximately 6 cm in diameter and reducible. The patient reports significant discomfort and a sensation of prolapse, indicating the need for surgical repair.
2. **Status post sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy and Hartmann’s pouch (November 2007):** Performed emergently for perforated diverticulitis. The patient is requesting elective colostomy reversal, which is clinically reasonable pending anatomical and functional evaluation of the distal colon.
3. **Tobacco use disorder:** Active smoker (1 pack/day for 15 years). This is a major modifiable risk factor that significantly increases the likelihood of postoperative wound complications, anastomotic leak, and hernia recurrence. 
4. **Questionable hypertension:** Current blood pressure is 135/79, which is borderline but currently does not require pharmacologic intervention; however, it warrants monitoring.
5. **Gastroesophageal reflux disease:** Currently asymptomatic and not requiring active intervention.

**PLAN:**

1. **Imaging Studies:** 
   - **CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast:** To evaluate the anatomy and fascial defects of the incisional hernia, assess the length and condition of the retained Hartmann’s pouch, and rule out any other intra-abdominal pathology prior to surgical intervention.
2. **Procedures:** 
   - **Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy:** To evaluate the mucosa of the remaining distal colon and Hartmann’s pouch, ensuring there are no strictures, active inflammation, or other contraindications to a safe anastomosis.
3. **Laboratory Tests:** 
   - Basic preoperative panel: Complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT).
4. **Medications / Preventive Care:** 
   - **Smoking Cessation:** Extensive counseling on the critical importance of quitting smoking prior to surgery to optimize wound healing and reduce the risk of hernia recurrence and anastomotic complications. Offer nicotine replacement therapy (e.g., nicotine patch or gum) and provide educational materials/referrals to a smoking cessation program.
5. **Referrals / Consultations:** 
   - **Social Work / Financial Counseling:** Refer immediately to assist the patient in applying for hospital charity care, Medicaid, or other state/federal assistance programs, given his current unemployed and uninsured status. This is essential to ensure he can safely proceed with the necessary surgical care.
6. **Follow-up:** 
   - Return to clinic in 3–4 weeks to review the CT and endoscopy results, discuss the risks, benefits, and alternatives of a combined incisional hernia repair and colostomy reversal, and assess progress on smoking cessation.

**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Recurrent Bilateral Hallux Valgus (Bunion) Deformity, Right Greater Than Left:** Status post prior bunionectomy approximately 13 years ago. Right foot weight-bearing radiographs confirm a recurrent, moderate-to-severe deformity with a 45-degree hallux abducto valgus (HAV) angle, 15-degree intermetatarsal (IMA) angle, and significant fibular sesamoid shift, without evidence of first MTP joint arthrosis. 
2. **Right Second MTP Joint Pain / Transfer Metatarsalgia:** Likely secondary to altered forefoot biomechanics and lateral column overload resulting from the recurrent first ray deformity, pes planus, and generalized hypermobility.
3. **Recurrent Lesser Toe Deformities:** Mild claw toe deformity of the left 2nd and 3rd toes, and the right 2nd toe, status post prior bilateral 2nd digit arthroplasties.
4. **Severe Pes Planus with Generalized Foot Hypermobility:** Contributing to the progressive nature of the forefoot deformities and mechanical symptoms.

**PLAN:**

1. **Imaging:** 
   - Obtain 3-view weight-bearing X-rays of the **left foot** to fully evaluate the extent of the recurrent deformity and facilitate comprehensive, bilateral surgical planning, as the patient has progressive symptoms on the left as well.

2. **Conservative Management (Interim):**
   - **Footwear/Orthotics:** Continue use of functional custom orthotics to support the medial longitudinal arch and offload the forefoot. Advise wearing shoes with a wide, deep toe box and a stiff sole to minimize MTP joint motion and reduce pressure on the lesser toes.
   - **Medications:** Trial of over-the-counter NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen or naproxen) or acetaminophen as needed for pain and inflammation, assuming no contraindications based on her updated medical history. 
   - **Activity Modification:** Encourage periodic rest and elevation when possible during her hospital shifts to reduce dependent edema and mechanical stress.

3. **Surgical Considerations:** 
   - Given the patient's occupational demands (prolonged standing), progressive deformity, and incomplete relief with optimized conservative measures, surgical correction is a reasonable and indicated next step. 
   - Discussed the risks, benefits, and alternatives of revision hallux valgus surgery. Given the generalized hypermobility, pes planus, and recurrent nature of the deformity, a first tarsometatarsal (TMT) arthrodesis (Lapidus procedure) or a proximal metatarsal osteotomy may be required to adequately correct the IMA and stabilize the first ray. Concurrent revision of the lesser toe deformities may also be discussed based on the left foot radiographic findings.

4. **Follow-up:** 
   - Return to the clinic in 4 weeks with the new left foot X-rays to review imaging, finalize the surgical plan, and discuss preoperative medical clearance if she elects to proceed with surgery. 
   - Instructed to return sooner if pain becomes acutely worse, or if she develops any skin breakdown, ulceration, or signs of infection over the prominent bunion or lesser toes.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Progressive dementia with gait impairment and urinary incontinence:** The patient’s initial presentation raised suspicion for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). However, his documented lack of clinical improvement following a trial of CSF drainage (temporary spinal catheter) strongly argues against iNPH and indicates he is not a candidate for ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting. 
2. **Probable neurodegenerative disease:** His progressive cognitive decline (MMSE dropped from 20-28/30 a year ago to 14/30 today), apathy, ideomotor apraxia, paratonia (gegenhalten), and new-onset impairment of upgaze are highly suggestive of a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Differential diagnoses include Alzheimer’s disease, Lewy body dementia, or an atypical parkinsonian syndrome (e.g., progressive supranuclear palsy). The progressive ventriculomegaly seen on the recent CT scan, in the absence of significant cortical atrophy and with a negative prior tap test, is most consistent with *hydrocephalus ex vacuo* secondary to this underlying neurodegenerative process.
3. **Status post cervical laminectomy and fusion:** The lack of gait improvement following his cervical spine surgery further supports that his severe gait disorder is of central/neurodegenerative origin rather than residual cervical myelopathy.
4. **Polypharmacy / Adverse medication effects:** The patient is currently taking promethazine as needed. This medication has strong anticholinergic and antidopaminergic properties, which are highly likely to exacerbate his cognitive impairment, gait instability, and parkinsonian features, and increase his risk of falls.

**PLAN:**

1. **Neurosurgical Intervention:** Discussed with the patient’s wife and daughter that a VP shunt is not recommended. Given the negative response to prior CSF drainage, a shunt is highly unlikely to provide clinical benefit and would expose this frail, elderly patient to unnecessary surgical and anesthetic risks. 
2. **Medication Adjustments:** 
   - **Discontinue promethazine** immediately due to its adverse cognitive and motor side effects in the elderly.
   - Continue Aricept, citalopram, and carbidopa/levodopa for now. However, the clinical benefit of carbidopa/levodopa is uncertain in this context. We will monitor his motor and cognitive status after stopping promethazine and can consider tapering the carbidopa/levodopa at the next visit if no clear benefit is observed.
   - Continue his bowel regimen (Colace, senna) and other maintenance medications (finasteride, tamsulosin, omeprazole, multivitamin) as tolerated.
3. **Diagnostics:** No further neuroimaging or invasive diagnostic testing (e.g., repeat lumbar puncture) is indicated at this time. The diagnosis is clinical, and further testing would be low-value and unlikely to alter our current management plan.
4. **Supportive Care:** Continue residence and care at the skilled nursing facility. Reinforce the need for maximal assistance with transfers and ambulation (wheelchair use) to prevent falls, as well as continued incontinence care. 
5. **Follow-up:** Return to clinic in 6 months for re-evaluation, or sooner if there are acute changes in his neurologic, functional, or behavioral status.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Coronary Artery Disease / Secondary Cardiovascular Prevention:** The patient is on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) and a statin, consistent with a history of CAD, prior stent, or cerebrovascular disease. She appears clinically stable based on the unchanged medication list. 
2. **Hypertension and Heart Failure:** Managed with an ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) and dual diuretic therapy (hydrochlorothiazide and furosemide). This regimen requires careful monitoring of volume status, blood pressure, and renal function. 
3. **Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus:** Requires ongoing monitoring of glycemic control. The combination of insulin therapy and fall risk necessitates strict avoidance of hypoglycemia.
4. **Hypothyroidism:** Stable on levothyroxine replacement.
5. **Fall Risk:** The patient is identified as a fall risk. This is a critical concern given her complex medication regimen. The combination of multiple antihypertensives and diuretics places her at high risk for orthostatic hypotension and volume depletion. Additionally, diabetic neuropathy or general deconditioning may be contributing factors. 

**PLAN:**

**1. Laboratory Studies (Targeted, high-value monitoring):**
*   **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP):** To monitor renal function (BUN, creatinine) and electrolytes (potassium, sodium), which is essential given the concurrent use of an ACE inhibitor, a thiazide diuretic, and a loop diuretic.
*   **Hemoglobin A1c:** To assess overall glycemic control and ensure the insulin regimen is appropriate without causing hypoglycemia.
*   **Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH):** To verify euthyroid status on the current levothyroxine dose.
*   **Fasting Lipid Panel:** To ensure LDL cholesterol remains at goal (<70 mg/dL) for secondary cardiovascular prevention.

**2. Medications:**
*   Continue current regimen: aspirin, clopidogrel (Plavix), levothyroxine, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide (Lasix), insulin, and simvastatin. 
*   **Counseling:** Educated the patient on recognizing early signs of orthostatic hypotension (e.g., dizziness or lightheadedness when standing) and hypoglycemia. Advised rising slowly from seated or lying positions.

**3. Fall Risk Mitigation:**
*   Reviewed comprehensive fall precautions, including ensuring adequate home lighting, removing loose rugs/trip hazards, and wearing supportive footwear.
*   **Referral:** Referral to Physical Therapy for a formal gait and balance assessment, strengthening exercises, and evaluation for assistive devices (e.g., cane or walker) if not already in place.
*   Will check orthostatic vital signs at the next in-person visit to evaluate for medication-induced hypotension. If symptomatic orthostasis is present, we will consider cautiously titrating down the diuretic or antihypertensive regimen.

**4. Follow-up:**
*   Return to clinic in 3 to 6 months to review laboratory results and assess clinical status.
*   **Return precautions:** Instructed to call the clinic or seek urgent care if she experiences a fall, recurrent dizziness, chest pain, new or worsening shortness of breath, or symptoms of hypoglycemia.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**

1. **Preoperative Medical Evaluation:** 54-year-old obese female with multiple comorbidities requiring medical optimization and risk stratification prior to planned surgery. 
2. **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus:** Currently managed with an insulin regimen and pioglitazone (Actos). Glycemic control requires objective assessment to minimize perioperative wound healing and infection risks.
3. **Obesity with Suspected Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA):** The patient is obese and reports heavy snoring. This places her at high perioperative risk for airway complications and postoperative respiratory depression, warranting formal evaluation.
4. **History of Stroke:** Patient reports no significant residual deficits, though the exam notes possible slight left arm weakness. She is on aspirin 81 mg daily. Perioperative antiplatelet management must be explicitly defined with the surgical and anesthesia teams.
5. **History of Hepatitis:** Etiology and current activity are unknown. Given her obesity and diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a strong possibility, but viral hepatitis must be ruled out.
6. **Multiple Joint Pains:** Differential diagnosis includes osteoarthritis (secondary to obesity) versus an inflammatory arthropathy. Notably, the patient is prescribed CellCept (mycophenolate mofetil), an immunosuppressant. The indication for this medication (e.g., underlying autoimmune disease, prior transplant) is unclear and requires urgent clarification to assess perioperative infection risk and determine if perioperative medication adjustments are needed.
7. **Hypertension and Hypercholesterolemia:** Currently on rosuvastatin (Crestor). Blood pressure control needs verification and optimization.

---

**PLAN:**

**1. Laboratory Tests:**
*   **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP):** Including liver function tests (LFTs) to evaluate the history of hepatitis.
*   **Hepatitis Panel:** Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies to determine etiology.
*   **Hemoglobin A1c:** To assess current diabetes control.
*   **Fasting Lipid Panel:** To evaluate current hypercholesterolemia management.
*   **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** Baseline preoperative evaluation.

**2. Imaging / Diagnostic Studies:**
*   **Resting 12-lead ECG:** Indicated for preoperative risk stratification given her age, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and prior stroke.
*   **Polysomnography (Sleep Study):** Referral for outpatient evaluation of suspected OSA. Identifying and managing OSA is critical for safe anesthesia planning and postoperative monitoring.

**3. Medications:**
*   **Continue current home medications:** Aspirin 81 mg daily, Rosuvastatin (Crestor) 10 mg daily, Pioglitazone (Actos) 15 mg daily, and her prescribed insulin regimen. 
*   **CellCept (mycophenolate mofetil) 500 mg twice daily:** Continue for now, but urgently clarify the indication with the patient or by obtaining outside medical records. If prescribed for an autoimmune/rheumatologic condition, coordinate with the prescribing specialist regarding perioperative holding or continuation protocols.
*   **Perioperative Planning:** Finalize specific perioperative medication adjustments (e.g., day-of-surgery insulin dosing, aspirin management) in direct coordination with the surgical and anesthesia teams.

**4. Referrals / Consultations:**
*   **Preoperative Clinic / Anesthesia:** For comprehensive preoperative risk assessment, clearance, and airway evaluation.
*   **Sleep Medicine:** For formal evaluation and management of suspected OSA.
*   **Rheumatology (or relevant prescribing specialist):** To clarify the indication for CellCept and evaluate the etiology of her multiple joint pains.

**5. Follow-up:**
*   Return to clinic in 2–4 weeks to review laboratory results, clarify medication indications, and ensure medical optimization prior to her scheduled surgery.
*   **Return Precautions:** Advised to seek immediate emergency care for any new or worsening neurologic symptoms, chest pain, shortness of breath, or signs of infection.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT**

**1. Suspected Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH):** 
This 74-year-old woman presents with a progressive 6-month history of gait instability (widened base, unsteadiness, frequent falls) and mild subjective cognitive slowing with occasional word-finding difficulty. Although she lacks urinary incontinence and has a normal MMSE (30/30), her clinical presentation combined with MRI findings of mild ventriculomegaly, temporal horn expansion, and a bowed/effaced corpus callosum is highly suspicious for early or incomplete NPH. 

**2. Differential Diagnosis:** 
Includes vascular cognitive impairment, early neurodegenerative disease (e.g., Parkinson's disease, though she lacks festination, resting tremor, or rigidity), and age-related gait changes. 

**3. Fall Risk:** 
High risk secondary to gait instability, widened base, and history of falls resulting in fracture (right wrist in 2007). Exacerbated by the use of sedative-hypnotics (Ambien) which are no longer effective.

**4. Hypertension:** 
Mildly elevated at 154/72 mmHg today, currently managed with Toprol and Norvasc.

---

**PLAN**

**1. Diagnostic Procedures:**
*   **High-Volume Lumbar Puncture (CSF Tap Test):** Remove 30–50 mL of CSF. Perform objective pre- and post-procedure gait and cognitive assessments (e.g., Timed Up and Go, Tinetti) to evaluate for clinical improvement. A positive response would strongly support the diagnosis of NPH and predict a favorable outcome from shunt surgery.

**2. Referrals and Consultations:**
*   **Physical Therapy:** Refer for gait and balance training, as well as a home safety evaluation to minimize fall risk.
*   **Neuropsychology:** Refer for formal baseline cognitive testing to objectively quantify her subjective cognitive slowing and help differentiate NPH from other neurodegenerative or vascular dementias.

**3. Medication Management:**
*   **Insomnia:** Discontinue Ambien. It is no longer effective and poses a significant, unnecessary fall risk in elderly patients. Recommend sleep hygiene measures or a safer alternative (e.g., melatonin) if needed.
*   **Hypertension:** Continue Toprol 50 mg daily and Norvasc 5 mg daily. Blood pressure is mildly elevated; recommend she follow up with her primary care physician for routine monitoring and potential adjustment if consistently elevated.
*   Continue all other current home medications (Premarin, Aciphex, vitamins, and supplements).

**4. Safety and Fall Prevention:**
*   Strongly recommend the use of an assistive device (e.g., a rolling walker or cane) for stability during ambulation, given her widened base and history of falls. 

**5. Follow-up:**
*   Return to clinic in 2–4 weeks to review the results of the tap test and neuropsychological evaluation. 
*   If the tap test is positive, we will discuss the risks, benefits, and logistics of ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement.
*   **Return Precautions:** Instruct the patient and her husband to seek immediate emergency care if she experiences a severe fall, head trauma, or any acute neurological changes (e.g., sudden weakness, severe headache, or acute confusion).
